title: Chapter LVIII

teacherSummary.text: Walking out together, Elizabeth thanks Darcy for what he did for Lydia. He says he thought only of her, and renews his proposal; she accepts. They admit how each has changed: he was proud and selfish, she prejudiced. Lady Catherine's visit, he says, gave him hope.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LVIII,” how does Austen show the second proposal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LVIII develops the idea of the second proposal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter LVIII to complicate the reader's understanding of the second proposal. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LVIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the second proposal responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LVIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the second proposal. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: How have both characters changed, and who changed more? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include retrospections, outstrip, unexampled, annexed, narrowly. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Your retrospections must be so totally void of reproach, that the contentment arising from them, is not of philosophy, but what is much better, of ignorance.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: The act, or the faculty, of looking back on things past.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Proposals during walks were among the few private moments a courting couple had. Now, why does this chapter matter? Mutual change makes the resolution earned rather than merely romantic. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Plot.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
